The paper compares backprojection and iterative smooth reweighted L1-minimization methods for analyzing RCS measurement data using ISAR imaging.
Backprojection is a straightforward method for ISAR imaging, but it has inherent limitations in resolution and ambiguity.
The L1-minimization method can provide improved resolution compared to backprojection, but the accuracy of the extracted RCS can be lower.
The downrange resolution used in the simulations is 5 cm, defined by c0/(2B) where c0 is the speed of light and B is the frequency bandwidth.
The grid spacing used in the simulations is 1 cm.
The frequency range used in the simulations is 13.5-16.5 GHz in 41 steps, and the azimuth angle range is -5.7° to 5.7° in 41 steps.
The reweighting function D(Δr) used in the iterative smooth reweighted L1-minimization method is defined as 1-(Δr/d) if Δr<d, and 0 otherwise, where d is set to twice the grid spacing.

The purpose of the reweighting in the iterative smooth reweighted L1-minimization method is to suppress the largest non-zero coefficients and increase the sensitivity to identify smaller coefficients, promoting sparsity in the solution.
Four iterations of the reweighted L1-minimization are used for all examples shown in the paper.

The main conclusion is that backprojection is more robust and accurate for RCS extraction, but the iterative smooth reweighted L1-minimization method can provide higher resolution imaging when the scattering features cannot be resolved in the backprojection image.
The RCS and RCS amplitude are related by σ[m^2] = |y|^2.
The adjoint of the forward operator A, A^†, is used to find a solution for the image x in the backprojection method.
The problem to be solved in the L1-minimization method is formulated as minimizing ||x||_1 subject to ||Ax-y||_2 ≤ κ, where κ is an estimate of the misfit to the model.
The iterative smooth reweighted L1-minimization procedure collects the points associated with a scattering center into a cluster, and it converges in four iterations for the examples shown.
The smoothing function D is used to create a smoothed version of the image x, denoted as xD, which is then used to calculate the reweighting matrix W.
